Controlling the Gold(I)-Catalyzed 1,5-Allenene Reaction:
Construction of Fused Rings with Excellent Diastereoselectivity
Nina Semleit and Gebhard Haberhauer *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 9635 −9639 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: In the present study, the gold(I)-catalyzed reaction
of 1,5-allenenes was controlled in such a way that instead of a [2 +
3] cycloaddition, a 5- exo-cyclization with the formation of a
carbocation occurred. The latter could be trapped with both
oxygen and carbon nucleophiles. In the investigated system, fused
tricyclic frameworks with three contiguous stereocenters with
excellent chemo- and diastereoselectivity in up to 95% yield were
obtained.
T
he usage of gold complexes for the electrophilic activation
of carbon −carbon multiple bonds for attack by various
nucleophiles under mild conditions has been intensively
investigated over the past decade.
1−12 In addition to alkynes, 8
allenes represent one of the most frequently used substance
classes in the ﬁeld of homogeneous gold catalysis. 5,12−18 For
example, an intramolecular reaction of an allene unit with
heteronucleophiles such as oxygen or nitrogen derivatives leads
to a series of heterocyclic compounds. 16,17 In the case of
allenenes, the gold-activated allene unit attacks the double
bond of the alkene moiety, and an alkyl cation is formed.
14,19,20
The fate of this species depends on the relative position of the
allene and alkene units within the molecule, the substituents at
the multiple bonds, and the reaction conditions; that is, the
reaction could be terminated by either deprotonation or
nucleophilic attack. In general, the nucleophile is a carbon
atom of the allenic unit leading to a [2 + 2] or [2 + 3]
carbocycloaddition.
14 Whereas interception of the intermedi-
ate carbocation by heteronucleophiles was possible in the case
of 1,7-allenenes,
21 in nonactivated 1,5-allenenes, the cationic
intermediate Int1, which is formed through 6- endo-cyclization,
cyclizes to the gold carbene Int2 (Scheme 1 a).20,22,23 After
removal of the gold catalyst, bicycle 2 is obtained. Depending
on the substituent pattern, 2 can undergo further gold-
catalyzed cyclization reactions, leading to polycycles. 20,23 In
this work, we intended to favor the 5- exo-cyclization by
introducing an aromatic moiety stabilizing the benzylic cation
Int3. The latter could be transferred to the cyclopentene
derivatives 4 by an intermolecular nucleophilic attack of both
oxygen and carbon nucleophiles ( Scheme 1 b).
We have chosen the bicyclic allenenes 5 as model systems
for two reasons. On the one hand, these systems can be easily
prepared from alkynylnaphthol ethers by gold catalysis.
24 On
the other hand, the desired products 6 represent 6−6−5-fused
rings with multiple stereogenic centers, which are of great
interest because this structural motif is frequently found in
natural products and pharmaceutical compounds with
important biological properties. Examples are picropodophyl-
lone, ( −)-epipodophyllotoxin, ( −)-podophyllotoxin, and ster-
ostrein A
25 (Scheme 1 c). The latter is a terpenoid isolated
from Stereum ostrea and shows antimalarial and cytotoxic
activity.25 Picropodophyllone, ( −)-epipodophyllotoxin, and
(−)-podophyllotoxin are naturally occurring aryltetralin cyclo-
lignans belonging to the family of podophyllotoxins. 26 They
exhibit various biological activities ranging from insecticidal,
antifungal, antiviral, anti-in ﬂammatory, and neurotoxic activ-
ities to immunosuppressive and further properties.
26 The class
of podophyllotoxins is characterized by the presence of a
carbonyl or hydroxyl group and an electron-rich aromatic
compound in the 1,4-position at the central six-membered ring.
Because ( −)-epipodophyllotoxin is the aglycone of the
antitumor drugs etoposide and teniposide,
27−29 there have
been considerable e ﬀorts in developing methods to construct
such fused tricyclic frameworks. 30−33 The design of alternative
synthetic routes to diverse tricyclic sca ﬀolds with di ﬀerent
functionalities and stereocenters is therefore highly desired.
Previous work demonstrated, that 1,5-allenedienes and 1,5-
allenenes can be prepared in only one step via the Au-catalyzed
rearrangement of propargyl aryl ethers.
24,34 Because we have
some experience with the gold-catalyzed reactions of
haloacetylenes,
35−38 we have chosen chloroacetylene 7a as
the starting material, which should react toallenene 5a via a
gold(I)-catalyzed rearrangement ( Table 1 ). We then inves-
tigated the gold(I)-catalyzed reaction of 7a with[JohnPhosAu-

detect a single product with a yield of 87% after only 2 h of
reaction time (entry 1). Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)
spectroscopic studies revealed that, in fact, the 6 −6−5 cycle 6a
was obtained. The intermediary formed allenene 5a could not
be observed after this reaction time.
Subsequently, we tested a wide variety of phosphine ligands
to improve the yield, which was not successful (entries 2 −7).
The usage of a carbene ligand did not lead to a better yield
despite varying the counterions (entries 8 −10). The catalyst
dichloro(2-picolinato)gold(III)
40 exclusively lead to the
formation of 5a in 88% yield (entry 11). Because the ligand
JohnPhos achieved the highest yield, we subsequently varied
the counterion
41 of this catalyst. Again, no improvement in the
yield was achieved (entries 12 −14). The usage of chloroform
as a solvent proved to be the most suitable compared with
DCM and DCE (entries 15 and 16). From these results, we
concluded that an optimum yield is obtained with a ratio of 7a
(0.1 M) to methanol of 1:2, the catalyst [JohnPhosAu-
(NCMe)]SbF
6 (5 mol %) in chloroform at room temperature,
and a reaction time of 2 h. Using these conditions, the reaction
can also be performed on a millimole scale.
To demonstrate that the reaction proceeds via allenene 5a as
an intermediate, we isolated the latter starting from acetylene
7a with dichloro(2-picolinato)gold(III) in 98% yield ( Scheme
2). Analogously, we were able to obtain allenenes 5b−d in
good to excellent yields. If the allenenes 5a−d were now
reacted in a second step with methanol and [JohnPhosAu-
(NCMe)]SbF
6, then cycles 6a−d were obtained ( Scheme 3 ).
Accordingly, allenenes 5 were the starting materials of the
subsequent cyclization. Because the yields of cycles 6a−d are
independent of whether the reaction starts from the acetylenes
7a−d or the intermediate allenenes 5a−d, acetylenes 7a−d are
often directly converted to avoid the isolation step of the
corresponding allenenes.
Next, we wanted to evaluate the scope of the reaction by
varying the substituents and the oxygen nucleophile. Di ﬀerent
substituents on the alkyne unit of 7 were tolerated ( 6b−c).
The introduction of an electron-withdrawing substituent at the
two-position of the naphthol sca ﬀold also led to the desired
cycle 6d. Using the terminal alkyne (R ′ = H), a rearrangement
of the propargylic unit occurred ( Scheme S1 ). Starting from
chloroacetylene 7a and di ﬀerent aliphatic alcohols, we were
able to isolate the corresponding ethers ( 6a and 6e−6h)i n
good to very good yields. The introduction of phenols as
oxygen nucleophiles was successful, too ( 6i−6m). Using

propargyl alcohol as a nucleophile resulted in the formation of
cycle 6n with a yield of 68%. Interestingly, the cyclization and
subsequent reaction with the oxygen nucleophile proceeded
with excellent stereoselectivity. Only one of the possible
diastereomers could be isolated as an enantiomeric pair in all
cases. The stereochemistry of the product could be determined
by means of nuclear Overhauser e ﬀect spectroscopy (NOESY)
of the cycles 6e and 6g (Figures S7 and S8 ). Upon introducing
a stereogenic center to the propargylic unit ( 7e), we were able
to isolate two diastereomers ( 6x and 6x′; see Scheme S2) with
a ratio of 60:40. Thus the stereogenic center at the propargylic
unit barely in ﬂuenced the diastereoselectivity of the cyclization
reaction.
We were interested in the reaction with [JohnPhosAu-
(NCMe)]SbF
6 as a catalyst without the addition of a
nucleophile. Here the question arises of whether the benzylic
cation reacts intramolecularly to form a bicycle, as in the case
of the Au-catalyzed reactions of 1,5-allenenes described so far.
(See Scheme 1 a.) As a result, a mixture of two diastereomers
was isolated in good yields and identi ﬁed as ethers 8a and 8b
by mass spectrometry ( Scheme 3 ). They are probably formed
by the reaction of the benzylic cation with traces of water
present in the solvent. The thus-formed alcohol acts as a
nucleophile in the reaction with another benzylic cation.
Overall, yields of the cyclization were good to very good.
Particularly striking, however, are the low, <20% yields of
cycles 6j and 6m. Whereas in the case of 6m the additional
carbon nucleophile (double bond of the alkene) presumably
leads to a polymerization without isolable byproducts, a more
detailed analysis of the reaction of 7a with 4-methoxyphenol
shows that a second product ( 6j′) is formed. Thus both the
oxygen of the phenol and a carbon atom of the aromatic
system can act as a nucleophile. Analogous observations were
made for the usage of cresol as a nucleophile ( 6i and 6i′).
These results encouraged us to employ carbon nucleophiles
to trap the intermediary formed benzylic cation. Indeed, we
were successful by using alkenes and electron-rich aromatic
systems ( Scheme 4 ). Both react under addition, subsequent
deprotonation, and protodesauration. In the case of the
alkenes, this formally results in migration of the double
bond, leading to regioisomers ( 6o). Note that in all cases, the
addition of the nucleophile is highly stereoselective. For
aromatic compounds, Friedel −Crafts alkylation is carried out
according to the rules of second substitution on the aromatic
ring with the following tendency: The more electron-rich the
aromatic system, the higher the yields. For example, yields of
95% can be obtained using 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene ( 6u). As
in the case of the oxygen nucleophiles, only one diastereomer
can be isolated as an enantiomeric pair ( Figure S9 ).
To investigate the mechanism of the cyclization, we
performed quantum-chemical calculations by means of
B3LYP-D3BJ(SMD).
42−45 The results are summarized in the
catalytic cycle, which is shown in Figure 1 a. First, the gold
catalyst coordinates to the allene unit of 5a, resulting in the
gold complex Int4. The latter is considered as a reference with
an energy of 0.0 kcal/mol. From there, two di ﬀerent routes are
possible. On the one hand, a [2 + 3] cycloaddition can take
place with the formation of the polycycle Int6. On the other
hand, cyclization is possible, yielding the formation of a ﬁve-
membered ring (Int5). A closer look at the calculated structure
of Int5 reveals a T-shaped edge-to-face π−π interaction
between the o-phenyl group of JohnPhos and the substrate
(Figure 1b). The distance between the centers of the aromatic
units amounts to 4.95 Å. 46 A comparison of the free energies

(ΔG) of the transition states shows that the 5- exo-cyclization is
signiﬁcantly more favored than the [2 + 3] cycloaddition
(+11.4 vs +17.4 kcal/mol). Therefore, only the 5- exo-
cyclization bearing an exocyclic cation occurs. The latter is
stabilized by the adjacent aromatic system and can react with a
nucleophile to form the product 6a. The stereoselectivity of
the reaction can be explained by looking more closely at Int5,
where the catalyst shields one side of the cation (C1 atom in
Figure 1b). Thus the attack of the nucleophile is possible only
from the opposite side, which explains the excellent stereo-
selectivity. Calculations using the small nucleophile MeOH
show an energy di ﬀerence of the transition states (nucleophilic
attack from the top and the bottom) of >8 kcal/mol. This
corresponds to an exclusive reaction from the upper side,
which was also observed in the experimental procedures.
In conclusion, we have successfully demonstrated that the
gold(I)-catalyzed reaction of nonactivated 1,5-allenenes can be
controlled. Normally, this reaction leads, via [2 + 3]
cycloaddition, to bicyclic and, in further steps, to polycyclic
compounds. We showed that the introduction of an aromatic
substituent leads to a 5- exo-cyclization with the formation of a
carbocation. The latter can react with both oxygen and carbon
nucleophiles. Starting from a bicyclic system, which can be
prepared in situ from a naphthol derivative, 6 −6−5-fused rings
exhibiting three stereocenters with excellent chemo- and
diastereoselectivity were obtained. Because of the very good
yields, this reaction provides a new facile and straightforward
approach for the diversity-oriented synthesis of such 6 −6−5-
fused rings.

Controlling the Gold(I)-Catalyzed 1,5-Allenene Reaction:
Construction of Fused Rings with Excellent Diastereoselectivity
Nina Semleit and Gebhard Haberhauer *

ABSTRACT: In the present study, the gold(I)-catalyzed reaction
of 1,5-allenenes was controlled in such a way that instead of a [2 +
3] cycloaddition, a 5- exo-cyclization with the formation of a
carbocation occurred. The latter could be trapped with both
oxygen and carbon nucleophiles. In the investigated system, fused
tricyclic frameworks with three contiguous stereocenters with
excellent chemo- and diastereoselectivity in up to 95% yield were
obtained.
T
he usage of gold complexes for the electrophilic activation
of carbon −carbon multiple bonds for attack by various
nucleophiles under mild conditions has been intensively
investigated over the past decade.
1−12 In addition to alkynes, 8
allenes represent one of the most frequently used substance
classes in the ﬁeld of homogeneous gold catalysis. 5,12−18 For
example, an intramolecular reaction of an allene unit with
heteronucleophiles such as oxygen or nitrogen derivatives leads
to a series of heterocyclic compounds. 16,17 In the case of
allenenes, the gold-activated allene unit attacks the double
bond of the alkene moiety, and an alkyl cation is formed.
14,19,20
The fate of this species depends on the relative position of the
allene and alkene units within the molecule, the substituents at
the multiple bonds, and the reaction conditions; that is, the
reaction could be terminated by either deprotonation or
nucleophilic attack. In general, the nucleophile is a carbon
atom of the allenic unit leading to a [2 + 2] or [2 + 3]
carbocycloaddition.
14 Whereas interception of the intermedi-
ate carbocation by heteronucleophiles was possible in the case
of 1,7-allenenes,
21 in nonactivated 1,5-allenenes, the cationic
intermediate Int1, which is formed through 6- endo-cyclization,
cyclizes to the gold carbene Int2 (Scheme 1 a).20,22,23 After
removal of the gold catalyst, bicycle 2 is obtained. Depending
on the substituent pattern, 2 can undergo further gold-
catalyzed cyclization reactions, leading to polycycles. 20,23 In
this work, we intended to favor the 5- exo-cyclization by
introducing an aromatic moiety stabilizing the benzylic cation
Int3. The latter could be transferred to the cyclopentene
derivatives 4 by an intermolecular nucleophilic attack of both
oxygen and carbon nucleophiles ( Scheme 1 b).
We have chosen the bicyclic allenenes 5 as model systems
for two reasons. On the one hand, these systems can be easily
prepared from alkynylnaphthol ethers by gold catalysis.
24 On
the other hand, the desired products 6 represent 6−6−5-fused
rings with multiple stereogenic centers, which are of great
interest because this structural motif is frequently found in
natural products and pharmaceutical compounds with
important biological properties. Examples are picropodophyl-
lone, ( −)-epipodophyllotoxin, ( −)-podophyllotoxin, and ster-
ostrein A
25 (Scheme 1 c). The latter is a terpenoid isolated
from Stereum ostrea and shows antimalarial and cytotoxic
activity.25 Picropodophyllone, ( −)-epipodophyllotoxin, and
(−)-podophyllotoxin are naturally occurring aryltetralin cyclo-
lignans belonging to the family of podophyllotoxins. 26 They
exhibit various biological activities ranging from insecticidal,
antifungal, antiviral, anti-in ﬂammatory, and neurotoxic activ-
ities to immunosuppressive and further properties.
26 The class
of podophyllotoxins is characterized by the presence of a
carbonyl or hydroxyl group and an electron-rich aromatic
compound in the 1,4-position at the central six-membered ring.
Because ( −)-epipodophyllotoxin is the aglycone of the
antitumor drugs etoposide and teniposide,
27−29 there have
been considerable e ﬀorts in developing methods to construct
such fused tricyclic frameworks. 30−33 The design of alternative
synthetic routes to diverse tricyclic sca ﬀolds with di ﬀerent
functionalities and stereocenters is therefore highly desired.
Previous work demonstrated, that 1,5-allenedienes and 1,5-
allenenes can be prepared in only one step via the Au-catalyzed
rearrangement of propargyl aryl ethers.
24,34 Because we have
some experience with the gold-catalyzed reactions of
haloacetylenes,
35−38 we have chosen chloroacetylene 7a as
the starting material, which should react toallenene 5a via a
gold(I)-catalyzed rearrangement ( Table 1 ). We then inves-
tigated the gold(I)-catalyzed reaction of 7a with[JohnPhosAu-

Subsequently, we tested a wide variety of phosphine ligands

The usage of a carbene ligand did not lead to a better yield
despite varying the counterions (entries 8 −10). The catalyst
dichloro(2-picolinato)gold(III)

formation of 5a in 88% yield (entry 11). Because the ligand

the counterion
41 of this catalyst. Again, no improvement in the

as a solvent proved to be the most suitable compared with
DCM and DCE (entries 15 and 16). From these results, we
concluded that an optimum yield is obtained with a ratio of 7a
(0.1 M) to methanol of 1:2, the catalyst [JohnPhosAu-
(NCMe)]SbF
6 (5 mol %) in chloroform at room temperature,
and a reaction time of 2 h. Using these conditions, the reaction
can also be performed on a millimole scale.
To demonstrate that the reaction proceeds via allenene 5a as
an intermediate, we isolated the latter starting from acetylene
7a with dichloro(2-picolinato)gold(III) in 98% yield ( Scheme
2). Analogously, we were able to obtain allenenes 5b−d in
good to excellent yields. If the allenenes 5a−d were now
reacted in a second step with methanol and [JohnPhosAu-
(NCMe)]SbF
6, then cycles 6a−d were obtained ( Scheme 3 ).
Accordingly, allenenes 5 were the starting materials of the
subsequent cyclization. Because the yields of cycles 6a−d are
independent of whether the reaction starts from the acetylenes
7a−d or the intermediate allenenes 5a−d, acetylenes 7a−d are
often directly converted to avoid the isolation step of the
corresponding allenenes.
Next, we wanted to evaluate the scope of the reaction by
varying the substituents and the oxygen nucleophile. Di ﬀerent
substituents on the alkyne unit of 7 were tolerated ( 6b−c).
The introduction of an electron-withdrawing substituent at the
two-position of the naphthol sca ﬀold also led to the desired
cycle 6d. Using the terminal alkyne (R ′ = H), a rearrangement
of the propargylic unit occurred ( Scheme S1 ). Starting from
chloroacetylene 7a and di ﬀerent aliphatic alcohols, we were
able to isolate the corresponding ethers ( 6a and 6e−6h)i n
good to very good yields. The introduction of phenols as
oxygen nucleophiles was successful, too ( 6i−6m). Using

cycle 6n with a yield of 68%. Interestingly, the cyclization and
subsequent reaction with the oxygen nucleophile proceeded
with excellent stereoselectivity. Only one of the possible
diastereomers could be isolated as an enantiomeric pair in all
cases. The stereochemistry of the product could be determined
by means of nuclear Overhauser e ﬀect spectroscopy (NOESY)
of the cycles 6e and 6g (Figures S7 and S8 ). Upon introducing
a stereogenic center to the propargylic unit ( 7e), we were able
to isolate two diastereomers ( 6x and 6x′; see Scheme S2) with
a ratio of 60:40. Thus the stereogenic center at the propargylic
unit barely in ﬂuenced the diastereoselectivity of the cyclization
reaction.
We were interested in the reaction with [JohnPhosAu-
(NCMe)]SbF
6 as a catalyst without the addition of a
nucleophile. Here the question arises of whether the benzylic
cation reacts intramolecularly to form a bicycle, as in the case
of the Au-catalyzed reactions of 1,5-allenenes described so far.
(See Scheme 1 a.) As a result, a mixture of two diastereomers
was isolated in good yields and identi ﬁed as ethers 8a and 8b
by mass spectrometry ( Scheme 3 ). They are probably formed
by the reaction of the benzylic cation with traces of water
present in the solvent. The thus-formed alcohol acts as a
nucleophile in the reaction with another benzylic cation.
Overall, yields of the cyclization were good to very good.
Particularly striking, however, are the low, <20% yields of
cycles 6j and 6m. Whereas in the case of 6m the additional
carbon nucleophile (double bond of the alkene) presumably
leads to a polymerization without isolable byproducts, a more
detailed analysis of the reaction of 7a with 4-methoxyphenol
shows that a second product ( 6j′) is formed. Thus both the
oxygen of the phenol and a carbon atom of the aromatic
system can act as a nucleophile. Analogous observations were
made for the usage of cresol as a nucleophile ( 6i and 6i′).
These results encouraged us to employ carbon nucleophiles
to trap the intermediary formed benzylic cation. Indeed, we
were successful by using alkenes and electron-rich aromatic
systems ( Scheme 4 ). Both react under addition, subsequent
deprotonation, and protodesauration. In the case of the
alkenes, this formally results in migration of the double
bond, leading to regioisomers ( 6o). Note that in all cases, the
addition of the nucleophile is highly stereoselective. For
aromatic compounds, Friedel −Crafts alkylation is carried out
according to the rules of second substitution on the aromatic
ring with the following tendency: The more electron-rich the
aromatic system, the higher the yields. For example, yields of
95% can be obtained using 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene ( 6u). As
in the case of the oxygen nucleophiles, only one diastereomer
can be isolated as an enantiomeric pair ( Figure S9 ).
To investigate the mechanism of the cyclization, we
performed quantum-chemical calculations by means of
B3LYP-D3BJ(SMD).
42−45 The results are summarized in the
catalytic cycle, which is shown in Figure 1 a. First, the gold
catalyst coordinates to the allene unit of 5a, resulting in the
gold complex Int4. The latter is considered as a reference with
an energy of 0.0 kcal/mol. From there, two di ﬀerent routes are
possible. On the one hand, a [2 + 3] cycloaddition can take
place with the formation of the polycycle Int6. On the other
hand, cyclization is possible, yielding the formation of a ﬁve-
membered ring (Int5). A closer look at the calculated structure
of Int5 reveals a T-shaped edge-to-face π−π interaction
between the o-phenyl group of JohnPhos and the substrate
(Figure 1b). The distance between the centers of the aromatic
units amounts to 4.95 Å. 46 A comparison of the free energies

signiﬁcantly more favored than the [2 + 3] cycloaddition
(+11.4 vs +17.4 kcal/mol). Therefore, only the 5- exo-
cyclization bearing an exocyclic cation occurs. The latter is
stabilized by the adjacent aromatic system and can react with a
nucleophile to form the product 6a. The stereoselectivity of
the reaction can be explained by looking more closely at Int5,
where the catalyst shields one side of the cation (C1 atom in
Figure 1b). Thus the attack of the nucleophile is possible only
from the opposite side, which explains the excellent stereo-
selectivity. Calculations using the small nucleophile MeOH
show an energy di ﬀerence of the transition states (nucleophilic
attack from the top and the bottom) of >8 kcal/mol. This
corresponds to an exclusive reaction from the upper side,
which was also observed in the experimental procedures.
In conclusion, we have successfully demonstrated that the
gold(I)-catalyzed reaction of nonactivated 1,5-allenenes can be
controlled. Normally, this reaction leads, via [2 + 3]
cycloaddition, to bicyclic and, in further steps, to polycyclic
compounds. We showed that the introduction of an aromatic
substituent leads to a 5- exo-cyclization with the formation of a
carbocation. The latter can react with both oxygen and carbon
nucleophiles. Starting from a bicyclic system, which can be
prepared in situ from a naphthol derivative, 6 −6−5-fused rings
exhibiting three stereocenters with excellent chemo- and
diastereoselectivity were obtained. Because of the very good
yields, this reaction provides a new facile and straightforward
approach for the diversity-oriented synthesis of such 6 −6−5-
fused rings.
